The ability to make fairly strong, direc- tional bonds by accepting electron pairs from neighboring mol­e­cules or ions is characteristic of the transition-metal elements. Coordination occupies a middle place energetically between the weak intermo­lec­u­lar attractions in molecular solids and liquids (see Chapter 10) and the stronger covalent and ionic bonding (see Chapters 3 and 6). Thus, heating blue vitriol disrupts the CuUOH2 bonds at tem­ peratures well below those required to break the covalent bonds in the SO4

22 group. The energy (more precisely, the enthalpy) required to break a M21UOH2 bond in a transition metal coordination complex falls in the range between 170 and 210 kJ mol21. This bond dissociation energy is far less than the bond energies of the stron­ gest chemical bonds (e.g., 942 kJ mol21 for N2), but it is by no means small. The bond dissociation enthalpy increases as the charge density on the metal atom in­ creases; Cu31 binds water more strongly than Cu21, for example.

A wide variety of mol­e­cules and ions bond to metals as ligands; common ones include the halide ions (F2, Cl2, Br2, I2), ammonia (NH3), carbon monoxide (CO), water, and a few other simple ligands listed in Table 8.3. Ligands that bond to a metal atom through a single point of attachment are called monodentate (derived from Latin mono, meaning “one,” plus dens, meaning “tooth,” indicating that they bind at only one point). More complex ligands can bond through two or more attachment points; they are referred to as bidentate, tridentate, and so forth. Ethyl­ enediamine (NH2CH2CH2NH2), in which two NH2 groups are connected by a hydrocarbon chain, is a particularly important bidentate ligand. Both nitrogen at­ oms in ethylenediamine have lone electron pairs to share. If all the nitrogen atoms in three ethylenediamine mol­e­cules bind to a single Co31 ion, then that ion has a coordination number of 6 and the formula of the resulting complex is [Co(en)3]31 (where “en” is the abbreviation for ethylenediamine). Complexes in which a ligand coordinates via two or more donors to the same central atom are called ­chelates (derived from Greek chele, meaning “claw,” because the ligand grabs onto the central atom like a pair of pincers).
